topic: The Pastry War, France vs Mexico 1838-39 (Remontel, San Juan de Ulúa, Santa Anna's leg)

slides.title: In 1838, France went to war with Mexico.

slides.kicker: It started with a looted bakery.
slides.body:
In 1832, during one of Mexico's many uprisings, a French pastry cook's shop in Tacubaya, then a town outside Mexico City, was looted. He blamed army officers.

The owner, known as Monsieur Remontel, asked for 60,000 pesos. Mexico said no.

slides.kicker: So he took his case to Paris.
slides.body:
His complaint joined a pile of older French grievances: unpaid claims, forced loans, trade restrictions.

In March 1838, France sent Mexico an ultimatum. It wanted 600,000 pesos in all.

slides.kicker: The pastry was a tenth of the bill.
slides.body: But it was the part people remembered. The conflict became known as the Pastry War.

In April 1838, the French navy blockaded the port of Veracruz.

On 27 November, its fleet bombarded the island fortress of San Juan de Ulúa. Mexico declared war.

On 5 December, Antonio López de Santa Anna was hit by French cannon fire. Part of his leg was amputated.

He buried it at his estate. In 1842, back in power, he gave it a state funeral. In 1844, rioters dug it up.

With a British diplomat mediating, Mexico agreed to pay the 600,000 pesos in instalments. The French fleet sailed home.

History kept the pastry shop. The pile of grievances behind it mostly faded.

slides.lead: A fight is rarely about the thing it's named after.
slides.accent: Look at what was piling up underneath.

slides.line: Save this for the next argument about the dishes.

caption:
The Pastry War of 1838–39 began with a looted French pastry shop near Mexico City. Behind it sat a 600,000-peso bill of French claims, a naval blockade of Veracruz, and a general who lost his leg, then gave it a state funeral.

What's the smallest thing you've seen start a much bigger fight?
